mainTopic: Four 'harder than' sayings, 'אילת השחר' and אסתר as the last miracle, when the early תמיד was slaughtered, and offerings performed at night
overview: This amud opens with four short sayings, each built as 'X is harder than Y' with a memory aid (סימן) from daily life: thoughts of sin, late-summer heat, a winter fever, and relearning forgotten Torah. Then רבי אבהו gives the verse source for רבי's view that dawn light spreads out, reading 'אילת השחר' in תהלים as comparing dawn to a deer's branching horns. Because that verse is linked to אסתר, רבי זירא explains why she is compared to a deer, and רבי אסי explains why she is compared to the dawn: her miracle was the last of all miracles. The גמרא challenges this with חנוכה and answers that פורים was the last miracle written into תנ״ך. For the view that אסתר was not given to be written, the verse is instead read as a lesson that the prayers of צדיקים keep being answered the more they pray. The גמרא then returns to the משנה and asks when the תמיד was slaughtered too early by moonlight. It answers that the mistake happened on a regular day, while the כהן גדול's immersion is the separate יום הכפורים procedure. Finally a ברייתא teaches that מליקה and קמיצה done at night are also disqualified. The גמרא begins to ask why the קומץ must be burned, and that question continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Thinking about sin is harder than the sin itself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא teaches that הרהורי עבירה (thoughts of sin) are harder than the sin itself, and gives a memory aid: the smell of meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: Thoughts of sin are harder than sin. Your memory aid is the smell of meat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a series of short sayings, each built as 'X is harder than Y.' This first one says that dwelling on a sin can be worse than doing it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is that a craving held in the mind can do more damage than the act itself. The סימן makes this concrete: the smell of roasting meat stirs up appetite more strongly than actually eating it. Thinking about something you want can affect you more than having it.

keyTerms.meaning: Thoughts or fantasies about sinning
Are harder, worse, or more harmful
And your memory aid (a סימן to help you remember)
The smell of meat

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean that thinking about a sin is punished more severely than doing it. The claim is about how much harm and pull the thought has on a person.

phrases.english: Thoughts of sin are harder than sin itself,
and your memory aid: the smell of meat.
phrases.notes: The smell of roasting meat whets the appetite more than eating it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the series of 'harder than' sayings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Thoughts of sin are harder than the sin itself.

steps.title: The end of summer is hotter than the summer itself
steps.stepSummary: Second saying in the series: the heat at the end of summer is harder to bear than the heat of the summer itself. The memory aid is an oven that has already been heated.
steps.simpleTranslation: The end of summer is harder than summer. Your memory aid is a heated oven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the series with a second 'harder than' saying, this time about weather.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By late summer everything has been soaking up heat for months, so the heat feels much heavier. The סימן is an oven that has been fired many times in one day: even a small new fire makes it extremely hot, because the heat has built up.

keyTerms.meaning: The end of (a period of time)
Summer
An oven that has already been heated

phrases.english: The end of summer is harder than summer,
and your memory aid: a heated oven.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second item in the same series of sayings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Late-summer heat is more oppressive than mid-summer heat.

steps.title: A winter fever is stronger than a summer fever
steps.stepSummary: Third saying in the series: a fever in winter is harder than a fever in summer. The memory aid is a cold oven.
steps.simpleTranslation: A fever in winter is harder than one in summer. Your memory aid is a cold oven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the third 'harder than' saying, about illness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Heating a cold oven takes a much stronger fire than heating a warm one. In the same way, a fever that manages to heat up the body in cold winter weather must be a stronger fever than one that does it in summer.

keyTerms.meaning: Fever
Winter
Cold

steps.confusionAlert: Notice that this goes the opposite way from step 2. There, the hot oven shows that built-up heat is worse. Here, the cold oven shows that heat which beats the cold must be stronger.

phrases.english: A fever of winter is harder than one of summer,
and your memory aid: a cold oven.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Third item in the series. It uses an oven image again, but the reverse case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A winter fever is more severe than a summer fever.

steps.title: Relearning forgotten Torah is harder than learning something new
steps.stepSummary: Fourth and last saying in the series: relearning old material you have forgotten is harder than learning new material. The memory aid is mortar made from old mortar.
steps.simpleTranslation: Learning old material again is harder than learning new material. Your memory aid is mortar from mortar.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the series with a saying about learning: going back to material you once knew and forgot is harder than learning something fresh.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Old, hardened mortar has to be crushed before it can be mixed again, which is more work than mixing new mortar. Forgotten learning works the same way: you have to break through the old, half-remembered version before you can rebuild it properly.

keyTerms.meaning: To learn or study
Old material (learning that was forgotten)
New material
Mortar or clay

steps.whatToRemember: All four sayings have the same shape: X is harder than Y, plus a סימן from everyday life (meat, a hot oven, a cold oven, mortar). The סימנים exist to help you remember each lesson.

phrases.english: Learning old material is harder than new material,
and your memory aid: mortar from mortar.
phrases.notes: Crushing hardened mortar and mixing it again is harder than mixing fresh mortar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Final item in the series of four sayings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Relearning forgotten material is harder than learning new material.

steps.title: The verse behind רבי's view that dawn light spreads out
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו gives the verse source for רבי's view that the light of dawn spreads in different directions. He reads 'אילת השחר' to mean that dawn branches out the way a deer's horns do.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: What is רבי's reason? As it is written, 'For the leader, about the morning deer.' Just as a deer's horns branch out here and there, so too dawn bursts out here and there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to an earlier discussion about the light of dawn. רבי אבהו shows where רבי's view comes from in a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי held that dawn light spreads out across the sky (and so is different from moonlight). The פסוק pairs 'deer' with 'dawn,' and רבי אבהו reads that pairing as a comparison: a deer's horns branch in many directions, and so does the dawn's light.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason or source?
The deer of the dawn (from תהלים 22)
Branch out, split apart
Bursts out, breaks through

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'רבי' with no other name means רבי יהודה הנשיא. רבי אבהו is not giving his own opinion; he is explaining where רבי's view comes from.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי,
phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said: What is the reason of Rabbi?
As it is written: 'For the leader, about the morning deer' (Psalms 22:1),

phrases.aramaic: מָה אַיָּלָה זוֹ קַרְנֶיהָ מַפְצִילוֹת לְכָאן וּלְכָאן,
phrases.english: just as this deer's horns branch out here and there,

phrases.aramaic: אַף שַׁחַר זֶה מַפְצִיעַ לְכָאן וּלְכָאן.
phrases.english: so too this dawn bursts out here and there.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the series of sayings and goes back to the earlier discussion about dawn light.
steps.raayaObject: רבי's view that dawn light spreads out in different directions.
steps.raayaSupportSource: תהלים 22:1, 'למנצח על אילת השחר,' read as comparing dawn to a deer's branching horns.

steps.title: Why אסתר is compared to a deer
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא explains why אסתר is compared to a deer: just as a deer stays as beloved to its mate as at the very first moment, אסתר stayed that beloved to אחשורוש.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: Why is אסתר compared to a deer? To teach you: just as a deer's womb is narrow and it is beloved to its mate every hour like the first hour, so too אסתר was beloved to אחשורוש every hour like the first hour.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the פסוק about 'אילת השחר' is applied to אסתר in מסכת מגילה, the גמרא adds a related teaching. רבי זירא explains the meaning of the 'deer' comparison.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The deer's narrow womb is taken as the reason it stays as desirable to its mate as it was at first. רבי זירא applies this to אסתר: אחשורוש's affection for her never faded.

keyTerms.meaning: Was compared, likened
Its womb is narrow
Beloved, desirable
Like the first moment

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא: לָמָּה נִמְשְׁלָה אֶסְתֵּר לְאַיָּלָה —
phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said: Why is Esther compared to a deer?

phrases.aramaic: לוֹמַר לָךְ: מָה אַיָּלָה רַחְמָהּ צַר
phrases.english: To teach you: just as a deer's womb is narrow
and it is beloved to its mate
every single hour like the first hour,

phrases.aramaic: אַף אֶסְתֵּר הָיְתָה חֲבִיבָה עַל אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ
phrases.english: so too Esther was beloved to Ahasuerus
every single hour like the first hour.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא: לָמָּה נִמְשְׁלָה אֶסְתֵּר לְאַיָּלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the 'אילת השחר' verse from step 5, now read as being about אסתר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אסתר is compared to a deer because she stayed as beloved to אחשורוש as she was on the first day.

steps.title: Why אסתר is compared to the dawn
steps.stepSummary: רבי אסי explains why אסתר is compared to the dawn: just as dawn is the end of the whole night, אסתר's miracle was the last of all the miracles.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אסי said: Why is אסתר compared to the dawn? To teach you: just as dawn is the end of the whole night, so too אסתר was the end of all the miracles.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second teaching on the same פסוק. רבי אסי explains the other half of the phrase, 'השחר,' as it applies to אסתר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זירא explained the word 'deer'; רבי אסי explains the word 'dawn.' Dawn closes the night, and the miracle of פורים closes the whole series of miracles. Taken simply, he says it was the last miracle of all, which is why the next step asks about חנוכה.

keyTerms.meaning: The end of the whole night
The end of all the miracles

steps.whatToRemember: So far the phrase 'אילת השחר' has been read three ways: as the source for רבי's view that dawn light spreads out (רבי אבהו), as a picture of אסתר's lasting favor (רבי זירא, the deer), and as a picture of אסתר as the last of the miracles (רבי אסי, the dawn). Steps 8–11 go on to challenge רבי אסי's reading and offer another one, about the prayers of צדיקים.
steps.whyThisMatters: This teaching is the basis for the well-known idea that the פורים story was the last of the miracles recorded in תנ"ך.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי: לָמָּה נִמְשְׁלָה אֶסְתֵּר לְשַׁחַר —
phrases.english: Rabbi Asi said: Why is Esther compared to the dawn?

phrases.aramaic: לוֹמַר לָךְ: מָה שַׁחַר סוֹף כׇּל הַלַּיְלָה,
phrases.english: To teach you: just as dawn is the end of the whole night,
so too Esther was the end of all the miracles.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי: לָמָּה נִמְשְׁלָה אֶסְתֵּר לְשַׁחַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pairs with step 6: רבי זירא explained 'deer,' and רבי אסי explains 'dawn.'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אסתר is compared to the dawn because her miracle was the last of all the miracles, just as dawn ends the night.

steps.title: But חנוכה came after פורים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי אסי's claim that אסתר's miracle was the last of all miracles, because the miracle of חנוכה happened later.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבי אסי from Step 7. How can פורים be the last miracle if חנוכה happened years afterward?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אסי said אסתר is like the dawn because dawn ends the night, and her miracle ended all miracles. But history shows a later miracle, חנוכה. So the claim 'last of all miracles' seems false.

keyTerms.meaning: The miracle of the חשמונאים, which happened after פורים
'But there is…', a short way of raising a counter-example

phrases.english: But there is Hanukkah!
phrases.notes: חנוכה happened after פורים, so פורים was not the last miracle.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבי אסי's statement in Step 7
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אסי's claim that אסתר's miracle was the last of all miracles
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Counter-example: חנוכה was a miracle that came later in history

steps.title: Last miracle that was written into תנ״ך
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא narrows רבי אסי's claim. פורים was the last miracle that was given to be written down as part of תנ״ך.
steps.simpleTranslation: We are speaking about miracles that were given to be written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question about חנוכה. רבי אסי meant the last miracle that was recorded in a book of תנ״ך.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer does not deny that חנוכה was a miracle. It limits 'last' to miracles that got a written book in תנ״ך. מגילת אסתר is such a book, and there is no book of חנוכה in תנ״ך.

keyTerms.meaning: Was given permission to be written as a holy book of תנ״ך
'We are saying', which tells you what was meant all along

phrases.english: We are saying [the last miracle] that was given to be written.
phrases.notes: Meaning the last miracle that was written into תנ״ך.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the scope of the original statement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: פורים was the last miracle of any kind
steps.terutzMaskana: פורים was the last miracle that was written into תנ״ך

steps.title: What about the view that אסתר was not given to be written?
steps.stepSummary: The answer from Step 9 works for those who hold מגילת אסתר is a holy written book. But there is a view that it was not given to be written. What does that view do?
steps.simpleTranslation: That works for the one who says אסתר was given to be written. But for the one who says אסתר was not given to be written, what can be said?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finds a gap in the answer from Step 9. That answer only works for one side of a debate about the status of מגילת אסתר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 depends on מגילת אסתר being a written holy book. One opinion holds it was not given to be written with that status. For him, פורים is not the last written miracle, so he needs another way to explain why אסתר is compared to 'אילת השחר'.

keyTerms.meaning: 'That works well for the one who says…', the opening of a challenge against the other view
'But for the one who says…'
'What can be said?', meaning how would he explain it

phrases.english: That works well for the one who says
Esther was given to be written.
But for the one who says
Esther was not given to be written,
what can be said?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנִיחָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר אֶסְתֵּר נִיתְּנָה לִכְתּוֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the answer in Step 9 does not work for every opinion
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer from Step 9 ('last written miracle')
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The answer depends on מגילת אסתר being a written holy book, which one view rejects

steps.title: The deer image is about the prayers of צדיקים
steps.stepSummary: The other view explains the verse through רבי בנימין בר יפת in the name of רבי אלעזר. The deer image teaches that the more צדיקים pray, the more their prayer is answered.
steps.simpleTranslation: He explains it like רבי בנימין בר יפת, who said in the name of רבי אלעזר: Why are the prayers of צדיקים compared to a deer? To teach you: as long as a deer grows, its horns keep branching out. So too, as long as צדיקים pray more, their prayer is heard.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 10. The view that אסתר was not given to be written does not read the verse as 'last miracle.' He reads it as a lesson about prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This view drops the 'dawn ends the night' idea. Instead the deer's always-growing horns stand for prayers that keep being accepted the more one prays. Applied to אסתר, it fits her many prayers being answered.

keyTerms.meaning: 'He explains it as…', meaning he reads the verse a different way
The prayers of the righteous
Branch out, split into more branches
Is heard, meaning accepted

steps.whatToRemember: There are two readings of 'אילת השחר' for אסתר. One says she was the last written miracle, like dawn ending the night. The other says prayers of צדיקים keep growing in power, like a deer's horns.

phrases.aramaic: מוֹקֵים לַהּ כְּרַבִּי בִּנְיָמִין בַּר יֶפֶת
phrases.english: He explains it according to Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet
[who] said in the name of Rabbi Elazar.
For Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet said
[that] Rabbi Elazar said:

phrases.aramaic: לָמָּה נִמְשְׁלוּ תְּפִלָּתָן שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים כְּאַיֶּלֶת —
phrases.english: Why are the prayers of the righteous compared to a deer?
To tell you:

phrases.aramaic: מָה אַיָּלָה זוֹ כׇּל זְמַן שֶׁמַּגְדֶּלֶת —
phrases.english: Just as this deer, as long as it grows,
its horns branch out,
so too the righteous:
as long as they pray more,
their prayer is heard.

steps.triggerLanguage: מוֹקֵים לַהּ כְּרַבִּי בִּנְיָמִין בַּר יֶפֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 10 by giving that view a different reading of the verse
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The deer and dawn image must mean פורים was the last miracle
steps.terutzMaskana: For this view, the deer image teaches that the more צדיקים pray, the more their prayer is answered

steps.title: When did the early slaughter of the תמיד happen?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה about mistaking moonlight for dawn and slaughtering the תמיד too early. Neither a regular day nor יום הכפורים seems to fit.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'They slaughtered the תמיד.' When did this happen? If on a regular day of the year, does it really have to be the כהן גדול? But if on יום הכפורים, is there moonlight then?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה. It asks when the moonlight mistake took place, and it shows that both possible answers have a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה mentions bringing the כהן גדול to immerse, which suggests יום הכפורים, since only then must he do the עבודה. But on the tenth of the month the moon is not shining near dawn in a way that could be confused with dawn. So a regular day fits the moonlight, and יום הכפורים fits the כהן גדול, but no single day fits both.

keyTerms.meaning: The daily morning קרבן
When?
'If you say…', the first option
'Is it impossible without…?', meaning is it really required
Moonlight

steps.confusionAlert: The words 'שחטו את התמיד' are a quote from the משנה, not a new statement. The גמרא quotes them only to ask about them.

phrases.english: [The Mishnah says:] They slaughtered the daily offering.
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה.

phrases.english: When?
If you say on the rest of the days of the year,
is it impossible without the High Priest?
phrases.notes: On a regular day, a regular כהן can do the service.

phrases.english: Rather, on Yom Kippur,
is there moonlight [at dawn then]?
phrases.notes: On the tenth of the month, the moon cannot be confused with dawn.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the אסתר discussion and returns to the משנה
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's story of the early slaughter followed by bringing the כהן גדול to immerse
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A dilemma: a regular day does not need the כהן גדול, and יום הכפורים has no moonlight at dawn

steps.title: The משנה is describing two separate things
steps.stepSummary: The משנה should be split in two. The mistake happened on a regular day. Then, separately, on יום הכפורים, once the watcher said 'ברקאי' they brought the כהן גדול to immerse.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it means: and on יום הכפורים, when the watcher said 'The light has flashed,' they brought the כהן גדול down to the place of immersion.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 12 by rereading the משנה. The part about the כהן גדול is a new, separate statement about יום הכפורים. It is not part of the story about the mistake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The moonlight mistake took place on a regular day, which solves the moon problem. The line about the כהן גדול is a separate rule for יום הכפורים: as soon as dawn is announced, he goes to immerse. Now each part fits its own day.

keyTerms.meaning: 'This is what it means', which introduces a rereading
'The light has flashed', the watcher's call that dawn has come
The place of immersion

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה has two parts. The moonlight mistake happened on a regular day. The immersion of the כהן גדול right after 'ברקאי' is the יום הכפורים procedure.

phrases.english: This is what [the Mishnah] is saying:
and on Yom Kippur, when [the watcher] said 'The light has flashed,'
they brought the High Priest down to the place of immersion.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Solves the problem from Step 12 by splitting the משנה
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the משנה as two separate statements
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The whole משנה describes one event on one day
steps.terutzMaskana: The mistake happened on a regular day, and the כהן גדול line describes the יום הכפורים procedure

steps.title: Pinching a bird or taking a handful at night also ruins the offering
steps.stepSummary: אבוה דרבי אבין teaches a ברייתא: the rule is not limited to the early-slaughtered תמיד. מליקת העוף and קמיצת מנחה done at night are also disqualified and must be burned.
steps.simpleTranslation: The father of רבי אבין taught: They did not say this rule only about the early-slaughtered תמיד. Even if a bird's neck was pinched at night, or a handful was taken from a מנחה at night, it must be burned.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that takes the rule from the משנה (an animal slaughtered at night is disqualified) and applies it to two more offerings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key act of a bird offering is מליקה, pinching the neck. The key act of a flour offering is קמיצה, taking out a handful. The ברייתא teaches that these acts are like slaughtering an animal: they must be done by day, and if they are done at night the item is disqualified and burned.

keyTerms.meaning: He taught (introduces a ברייתא)
Not only this did they say (the rule goes further)
Pinching the neck of a bird offering with the כהן's fingernail
Taking the handful from a flour offering
It must be burned (it is disqualified)

steps.confusionAlert: 'Burned' here does not mean burned on the מזבח as an offering. It means it is disqualified and burned as invalid, like the early-slaughtered תמיד.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that daytime is required not only for slaughtering animals, but also for the key acts of bird offerings (מליקה) and flour offerings (קמיצה).

phrases.english: The father of Rabbi Avin taught:
Not only this did they say,
phrases.notes: 'This' = the תמיד slaughtered before dawn, which is burned.

phrases.english: but even the pinching of a bird
phrases.notes: The way a bird offering is killed.

phrases.english: and the taking of a handful of a meal-offering at night
must be burned.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנֵי אֲבוּהּ דְּרַבִּי אָבִין לֹא זוֹ בִּלְבַד אָמְרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the משנה's case of the תמיד slaughtered at night and extends that rule to bird and flour offerings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מליקה and קמיצה done at night disqualify the offering, and it must be burned.

steps.title: The bird makes sense, but why burn the handful?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts the rule for the bird, since the pinching cannot be undone. It begins to ask why the קומץ should be burned. The question continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for a bird burnt-offering: what was done is done. But the handful...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts to challenge the ברייתא. This line sets up the difficulty, and the full question about the קומץ comes right on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once a bird has been pinched, it is dead, so the mistake cannot be fixed and burning makes sense. A handful of flour is different. The act did not destroy anything permanently. So the גמרא is about to ask why the handful cannot be fixed instead of burned.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense (granted) for this case. It sets up a contrast.
A bird brought as a burnt-offering
What was, was. It cannot be undone.
The handful of flour taken from a מנחה

steps.confusionAlert: The question is cut off at the end of the amud. Do not think the גמרא is finished. 'אלא קומץ' opens the real difficulty, which continues next.

phrases.english: Granted, a bird burnt-offering —
phrases.notes: The case that is easy to understand.

phrases.english: what was, was.
phrases.notes: The bird is already dead, so there is no fixing it.

phrases.english: but the handful,
phrases.notes: The question continues on the next amud: why can't it be fixed?

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא עוֹלַת הָעוֹף מַאי דַהֲוָה הֲוָה אֶלָּא קוֹמֶץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Analyzes the ברייתא from Step 14. It accepts the bird case and questions the קומץ case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that a קומץ taken at night must be burned.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Burning makes sense only when the mistake cannot be fixed. A pinched bird cannot be fixed, but a handful of flour seems like it could be, so why burn it?
